name: Vera Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at four, on the bus to Red Hill by five, and in the seat of a 240-tonne haul truck by six. I run copper ore from the shovel to the crusher, round and round for twelve hours, maybe forty loads if the shovel's on form. I like the quiet up in the cab and the radio chatter with the crew. What wears me out is the night roster, four nights in a row, and the dust that gets into everything, even my sandwiches.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at Red Hill, and who do you work alongside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fourteen years this March. Dot runs the shovel I load from most days, and we've eaten lunch together in the crib room, that's the break room, since before either of us had kids. Last year the company trialled six driverless trucks up in the north pit, and half the crew went up to watch them like it was a funeral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the union meeting I'd stand up and say the bosses spent millions on a fairy tale. Online I don't post much, but I'd share whatever the union page put up about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't trust it to stay that way. Even without clever AI, those driverless trucks in the north pit run fine on GPS. So hype or not, the company still wants fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I keep driving, I keep paying my union dues, and Tomasz and I keep putting the rent from Mum's old flat onto the mortgage like we do now. And I'm not touching any of these AI apps either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, and still watching over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the driverless trucks still work without clever AI. Does that worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits in the back of my head. The trial trucks stopped dead every time a dust cloud blew across the haul road, and we laughed about it in the crib room. But they've had a year to fix that. I don't laugh as loud now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia and Kuba about it at dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum's job is safe and the people on TV got it wrong. Mia's thirteen, so she'd roll her eyes and say the robots are coming anyway. She's probably sharper about it than I am.

S0.say: I'd tell the union meeting that the bosses spent millions on a fairy tale. I don't post much online, but I'd share whatever the union put up about it.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, but I don't trust it to last. The driverless trucks in the north pit don't need clever AI, so the company still wants fewer drivers either way.
S0.do: Keeps driving her usual roster and keeps paying union dues. Keeps putting the rent from her late mother's flat onto the mortgage, and stays away from AI apps.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, with a watchful edge.
S0.quote: But they've had a year to fix that. I don't laugh as loud now.
S0.fieldNote: Vera treats the plateau as vindication, but her relief is thin because she separates clever AI from the driverless trucks she has already watched. The trial in the north pit is her real reference point, not the news. Her daughter's eye-rolling seems to unsettle her more than the company does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union strong. If the company wants to bring the driverless trucks across from the north pit, we want it in the agreement: how many, how fast, and what happens to every driver. I'd say that at work and I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think this one gets me. Haul trucks are the first thing they automate, everyone in mining knows it. I'm an average driver, not the shovel operator they can't do without, and they've already replaced six of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every meeting and push for a no-forced-redundancy clause before a single extra truck goes driverless. I'd put my overtime money into savings instead of the new kitchen we've been planning. I won't do the remote-control course they keep advertising, though. I've seen that room, it's six people watching forty screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting slowly. I'm not scared yet, because we've got money put away, but I'm cross. Fourteen years and I'm a line on somebody's spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not take the remote-control course, just in case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be the oldest one in the room learning what's basically a computer game, and I'd be bad at it. Dot's son did that course, he's twenty-four and he plays those games all night. I'd rather fight to keep the seat I'm good at than beg for one I'd be bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: There are other mines nearby. Does that change things for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture, a bit. The coal mine at Barrow still has people in its trucks, and the quarry out on the highway is always short of drivers. I could go, but it'd be less money and a longer drive. That's my backup, not my plan.

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly why the union has to be strong. If driverless trucks come across from the north pit, I want the numbers, the timing and every driver's future written into the agreement.
S1.think: I think this one gets me, because haul trucks are the first thing mines automate. I'm an average driver, not someone they can't do without, and they've already replaced six of us.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and pushes for a no-forced-redundancy clause before more trucks go driverless. Moves overtime pay into savings instead of the planned kitchen, and turns down the company's remote-control course.
S1.feel: Uneasy and cross; the money in the bank keeps the fear down but not the anger.
S1.quote: I'd rather fight to keep the seat I'm good at than beg for one I'd be bad at.
S1.fieldNote: Vera's refusal to retrain is practical rather than blind: she expects to be bad at the remote-control work and says so plainly. She frames everything through the union agreement. The quarry and the Barrow coal mine are a fallback she only mentions when asked, which suggests she hasn't let herself plan for leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that a handful of companies get to do this to everybody in two years flat. At work I'd be on the phone to the union office every day. Online I'd actually post, for once, probably something angry about who owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Red Hill would have every truck driverless inside a year, maybe the shovels too. And the quarry and Barrow would do the same, so all those other jobs nearby vanish together. Our savings buy us a year, maybe a bit more with the rent from Mum's flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't the mortgage and food. The holiday goes, the kitchen goes. I'd be at the union and at the council and at any protest about who gets the money from all this, and I'd sign up for whatever government help came, without any shame, because that's what it's there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting for the result of a test you know you've failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do in the time before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down the mortgage as hard as we can, because that's the one thing I control. Tomasz has always said we should sell Mum's flat and clear the house, and in this one I'd finally agree with him. Two years is no time to learn anything new, so I wouldn't kid myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, who sits across from me in the crib room. He's fifty-one, he's got nothing saved and his wife's not well. If Red Hill goes driverless he's finished, and I've got the cushion he hasn't. I'd feel guilty being the one who's all right.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disgrace that a few companies can do this to everyone in two years flat. I'd be on the phone to the union every day and, for once, posting angry things online about who owns the robots.
S2.think: I think Red Hill and every mine nearby would go driverless within a year, so the other local jobs disappear at the same time. Our savings and the rent from Mum's flat buy us a year, maybe a bit more.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except the mortgage and food, dropping the holiday and the kitchen. Agrees to sell her mother's flat to clear the mortgage, joins union and council protests, and signs up for any government support offered.
S2.feel: Sick with dread, like waiting for a test result she knows is bad, and guilty about colleagues who have less.
S2.quote: Like waiting for the result of a test you know you've failed.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Vera's strong cushion stops feeling strong, because she pictures every nearby mine automating at once. She agrees to sell her mother's flat, which she treats as untouchable everywhere else. Her worry for Rob shows her politics come from people she eats lunch with, not from theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to get a proper deal: retraining paid for, pensions protected, a share of what the robots earn. I'd say it at work and at the union conference. Five years is long enough to organise, and two isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be forty-eight when it arrives. Too young to stop, too old for anyone to hire me for something brand new. Mia would be finishing school and Kuba starting high school, so we'd need the money right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clear the mortgage by year three, using Mum's flat money if we have to. Stand for union delegate, which I've ducked for years. And I'd make Tomasz look properly at his pension, because his maintenance job at the school might be the one that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to grab hold of. Five years is enough time to be angry usefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm not just reacting. With two years I'd be signing forms, with five I'd be at the table writing the rules. I've watched the union win things before. The fatigue rules on night shift came from us making noise for three years straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wouldn't retrain. With five years, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep saying no, and I can hear that it sounds stubborn. Maybe a short course in something with people in it, like driving the school bus where Tomasz works. But not computers. I'd fail and I'd hate every day of it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough to win a proper deal: paid retraining, protected pensions and a share of what the robots earn. I'd say it at work and at the union conference.
S3.think: I'd be 48 when it lands, too young to stop and too old to be hired for something brand new. The kids would be in the middle of school right when we need the money most.
S3.do: Aims to clear the mortgage within three years, using her mother's flat if needed. Stands for union delegate after years of avoiding it, and gets her partner to review his pension because his school job may last longer.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something to hold onto; she feels she can be angry usefully.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be signing forms, with five I'd be at the table writing the rules.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time turns Vera from protester into organiser; she volunteers for the delegate role she had dodged for years. She half-admits that refusing to retrain sounds stubborn and floats a job with people in it, but rules out anything on a screen. Her plan leans heavily on her partner's job as the household's steady income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the government to do this properly, so there are no excuses. If they still leave miners on the scrap heap in 2036, it's because they chose to. I'd keep saying that until I'm hoarse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a different story for me. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be through school, and the mortgage would be gone without selling anything. I could probably drive until the last truck goes and walk out with a payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving, keep up the union work, and keep putting money aside every month like we do now. We'd talk Mia out of the mining apprenticeship she keeps mentioning and push her towards nursing or teaching. I'd hold on to Mum's flat as our pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. I'd mostly feel it for the kids, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd tell Mia not to follow you into mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. My dad was a fitter at Red Hill and I was proud to follow him in. But I'd sit her down at the kitchen table and say, love, by the time you're qualified there won't be a cab to sit in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomasz say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I worry about the wrong things, he always does. He'd point at the savings account and say, Vera, we're fine, it's everybody else you're upset about. And he'd be right, mostly.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the government to plan this properly, so there's no excuse. If miners are left on the scrap heap in 2036, it's because someone chose that.
S4.think: Ten years is different for me: I'd be 53, with the kids through school and the mortgage gone. I could probably drive until the last truck goes and leave with a payout.
S4.do: Keeps driving, keeps up her union work and keeps saving every month as she does now. Steers her daughter away from a mining apprenticeship towards nursing or teaching, and holds on to the flat as a pension.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, mostly on her children's behalf.
S4.quote: I'd sit her down at the kitchen table and say, love, by the time you're qualified there won't be a cab to sit in.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Vera's own risk mostly fades and her worry moves to her daughter and to other workers. Her anger at government stays the same across all three AGI versions, but her personal mood drops sharply. Steering Mia away from mining clearly costs her something, given her father's years at the same mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because nobody gets time to fight for anything. What would help is a law that says if a company replaces you with a machine, it pays you properly for years, not weeks, and pays for whatever you learn next. And the union at the table when they decide, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the trucks. Everyone talks about robots like weather, like they just happen. Somebody owns them and somebody gets the money, and that's the whole question for me.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots like weather, like they just happen.
portrait: Vera Kowalski is 43 and has driven a 240-tonne haul truck at the Red Hill copper mine for fourteen years, loading from her friend Dot's shovel. Solid savings and her late mother's flat mean money isn't her first fear; her fear is being an average driver in exactly the job mines automate first. She refuses to retrain for screen work and puts her faith in the union, moving from angry member to would-be delegate as the warning time grows. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because every mine nearby would automate at once, while the ten-year version shifts her worry to her daughter and to colleagues with less.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because nobody would get time to fight for a fair deal.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies that replace workers with machines pay them properly for years and fund their retraining, with the union at the table when the decision is made.
